summary:
The Republic of Karelia stands under Russia's national framework, which sets the risk level for any transgender visitor. A 2023 law signed by President Vladimir Putin prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, effectively banning legal gender recognition and trans-specific healthcare; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition.

Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government warnings expressly advise LGBT travellers of this exposure.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records that LGB people are not assessed as generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while transgender people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The same note counts 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of any personal characteristic, citing the risk of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, with at least 20 people facing criminal charges since January 2024. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

No facts specific to the Republic of Karelia appear in the sources, and no regional divergence from the national framework is recorded for this division.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget over the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where roughly 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025.

Detention carries lethal risk in this context. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.

Geography conditions the assessment: the UK Home Office treats people in the North Caucasus, transgender people and public LGBT+ advocates as likely to face persecution, while its assessment for LGB people elsewhere in Russia is not the same. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is banned outright in Russia: the 2023 statute prohibits both gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since that year.

No statutory discrimination protection exists for LGBT+ people, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. Human Rights Watch counted 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

Of the 101 extremism-related convictions issued by 30 June 2025, 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, and three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment. Repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison.

Russia's anti-extremism machinery also reaches residents through administrative charges: Human Rights Watch recorded convictions both under the administrative code and the criminal code for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its alleged symbols.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports Karelia-specific arrests, court proceedings, regional enforcement patterns or local service provision; the division's position is derived entirely from the national framework, and the absence of regional detail is unresolved rather than evidence of lower risk.

Whether Karelia's courts have issued convictions under the extremist designation, and in what numbers, is not sourced here.

The US advisory's wording about wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement is stated at national level; no source specifies how these risks are applied at Karelia's border crossing points or airports.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) documents no division-specific facts, so the persecution assessment for transgender people applies to Russia as a whole without regional qualification.
